newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait parliament probes scandal, helps stability.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait parliament probes scandal, helps stability.

text.p: Kuwait, political odd-man-out among Gulf Arab states, draws the uneasy gaze of its neighbours next month by electing a body they would prefer to do without -- a parliament.
Only men may vote in the second assembly polls since the 1991 Gulf War, but in such a politically conservative region it is remarkable any country holds elections at all, Kuwaitis say.

The sharp-tongued chamber is no rubber stamp. It has taken painful bites out of government prestige throughout its 33 years of existence and in particular since the 1991 Gulf War, with tough probes into alleged corruption.
Some call parliament Kuwait's best-kept political secret.

The nearest it came to international prominence recently was when it was asked by Kuwait's government to approve the deployment this month of 3,500 U.S. troops in the latest security flare-up with former occupier Baghdad.
But while its international profile may be low, the assembly is the focus of bad-tempered domestic politics and notorious throughout the Gulf for the venom of its verbal exchanges.
Gathering weekly in a splendid chamber, MPs engage in a political blood-letting that horrifies neighbouring states reliant solely on ruling families or virtual one-party systems.
Walkouts, finger-pointing and shouting matches provide drama in moments when Kuwait's uneasy compromise between hereditary rule and popular participation temporarily breaks down.
But despite parliament's confrontations with the government and its dogged pursuit of more power, its existence has helped boost the country's overall political stability, diplomats say.
Six years after the turmoil of Iraq's 1990-91 occupation Kuwait is probably the most stable country in the Gulf because parliament provides a forum for people's views, diplomats say.
"Look at the unrest happening in Bahrain and elsewhere in the Gulf. Here in Kuwait we have this important safety valve," says Islamist opposition lawmaker Adnan Abdul-Samad.

The government headed by the ruling Sabah family is expected to work hard in the limited franchise, October 7 polls to wrest control of the chamber from opposition deputies whose war on corruption has earned them powerful enemies as well as fans.

Parliament's Islamists, liberals and independents have made their presence felt wherever Kuwaiti officials do business -- from Europe, to Asia and the United States -- by trying to monitor closely flows of public funds.

Much of their work is a reaction to Kuwait as it was run in parliament's absence in the late 1980s when, MPs allege, Kuwaiti officials presided over an orgy of kickbacks, influence-peddling and mismanagement that cost Kuwait billions of dollars.
MPs attribute the alleged graft to the absence of assembly oversight. Kuwaiti leaders dissolved parliament in 1986 during the Iran-Iraq war amid political and security tensions.
Kuwait was shaken by pro-democracy protests in early 1990 that police quelled with tear gas and opposition arrests.
The state revived parliament with elections in 1992, mindful that its human rights record was in the international spotlight after the 1991 Gulf War ended a seven-month Iraqi occupation.

MPs' targets have been high profile. Parliament was a key force behind the 1994 indictment of former oil minister Sheikh Ali Khalifa al-Sabah, by common consent the most gifted minister of his generation and once a major personality in world oil, on charges of earning illegal profits.
Sheikh Ali denies all charges. The trial continues.

Whatever the outcome of the polls, the prime minister is by tradition a Sabah member. But parliament's political complexion is important because Kuwaiti stability has traditionally depended on cooperation between the chamber and the government.
The opposition seeks more parliamentary control over the state machinery and more elected MPs serving in the cabinet - aims they are determined to pursue in the next assembly term.
MPs say some of the men they have pursued in their graft probe -- many of them in voluntary exile -- retain links to authority and seek to bring about a more docile parliament.
